name: Communication and Network Security
plainMeaning: This domain is about how information travels safely from one place to another. It covers how networks are built, which devices protect them, and how to stop attacks on the traffic.

topics.name: OSI and TCP/IP models
topics.simpleExplanation: Computers talk in layers, a bit like a letter. You write it, put it in an envelope, drop it in a mailbag, and a truck drives it away. The OSI model (Open Systems Interconnection) is a seven-layer teaching map of that journey. The TCP/IP model (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) is the four-layer version the internet really uses. Each layer does one job and adds its own label. Knowing the layers tells you where an attack happens and which control can stop it.

studyNotes.heading: Why we use layers, and the seven in order
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to see why networks are described in layers, and then learn the seven layers in their exact order.

A network conversation is a big job, and engineers split big jobs into small ones. Think about sending a parcel. One person packs it, another writes the label, another sorts it at the depot, and a driver carries it. The driver does not need to know what is in the box. The packer does not need to know the road.

Network layers work the same way. Each layer does one job. Each layer serves the layer above it and uses the layer below it. If one layer changes, the others should keep working. That is why you can swap a copper cable for Wi-Fi, and your web browser never notices.

The OSI model is the best known map of these layers. OSI stands for Open Systems Interconnection. It is a reference model, which means it is a teaching map and not a product you install.

Learn these seven layers in order, from the top down. The exam uses both the names and the numbers.

- Layer 7, Application.
- Layer 6, Presentation.
- Layer 5, Session.
- Layer 4, Transport.
- Layer 3, Network.
- Layer 2, Data Link.
- Layer 1, Physical.

A memory sentence from Layer 1 upward is this: Please Do Not Take Sweets, Pies, Apples. The first letters give you Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application.

Why does a security person care? Because layers let you ask one useful question. At what level is this problem, and which control works at that level?

Here is a workplace example. A company finds that someone has clipped a small device onto a cable in a wiring cabinet. A stronger password policy does nothing about that. The problem is at Layer 1, so the answer starts with a locked cabinet and regular inspection.

Here is what to take away. Layers split one big job into seven small jobs. Learn the order until it is automatic, and use it to match each problem with the right control.

studyNotes.heading: The top three layers and their protocols
studyNotes.body:
Now we will walk through the top three layers, looking at what each one does and which protocols live there. A protocol is simply an agreed set of rules for communicating.

Layer 7 is the Application layer. It is the doorway that programs use to reach the network. It is not the program itself. Your web browser is a program, but the rules it uses to ask for a page belong to Layer 7.

Here are the main Layer 7 protocols. HTTP is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, for web pages. SMTP is the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, for sending email. POP3 is Post Office Protocol version 3, and IMAP is the Internet Message Access Protocol. Both are for collecting email. FTP is the File Transfer Protocol. DNS is the Domain Name System, which turns names into addresses. SSH is Secure Shell, for a protected remote login. SNMP is the Simple Network Management Protocol, for looking after devices.

Layer 6 is the Presentation layer. It puts data into a form that both sides understand, much like a translator at a meeting. Its jobs are formatting, compression and encryption. Encryption means scrambling data to keep it secret. Examples are ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, which is a code for text, and JPEG, a picture format from the Joint Photographic Experts Group.

Layer 5 is the Session layer. It starts, manages and ends conversations between programs. Think of a phone call. You dial, you talk, and you hang up. Examples are RPC, which is Remote Procedure Call, and NetBIOS, the Network Basic Input Output System, an old naming and session service.

A word about TLS, which is Transport Layer Security and protects web traffic. It does not fit neatly into one layer. It runs on top of Layer 4 and serves the applications above it. So on the exam, choose the best fit among the options you are given.

Here is a workplace example. An attacker types harmful database commands into a web form. Every lower layer sees ordinary traffic. Only a control that reads Layer 7 content can notice the problem.

Your takeaway is this. Application is the doorway, Presentation is the translator, and Session is the phone call.

studyNotes.heading: The bottom four layers, protocols and devices
studyNotes.body:
Next we will cover the bottom four layers. These are where addresses, ports and hardware live, so the exam returns to them again and again.

Layer 4 is the Transport layer. It moves data from end to end and uses port numbers, which are like numbered doors into a computer. Its two main protocols are TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, and UDP, the User Datagram Protocol.

Layer 3 is the Network layer. It picks a path between networks using IP addresses. IP is the Internet Protocol. Other protocols here are ICMP, the Internet Control Message Protocol, which ping uses, and IGMP, the Internet Group Management Protocol, which manages multicast groups. IPsec, or IP Security, protects traffic at this layer. OSPF, which is Open Shortest Path First, is a routing method. Routers work here.

Layer 2 is the Data Link layer. It moves data between devices on the same local network, using MAC addresses. MAC stands for Media Access Control, and a MAC address is the hardware label on a network card. It has two sublayers, Logical Link Control on top and Media Access Control underneath. Examples are Ethernet and PPP, the Point-to-Point Protocol. ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, finds the MAC address that goes with an IP address, and it is usually placed here. Switches and bridges work here.

Layer 1 is the Physical layer. It sends raw bits as electricity, light or radio. Cables, connectors, hubs and repeaters belong here. A hub simply repeats every signal out of every port.

Think of a postal system. The street address on the envelope is like an IP address, because it gets the letter across the country. The name of the person inside the house is like a port number. And the local carrier who walks from door to door works like Layer 2.

Now a workplace example. A hub sends all traffic to every connected computer, so anyone plugged in can read it. A switch sends each frame only to the right port. Replacing old hubs with switches therefore reduces casual eavesdropping.

Here is what to take away. Ports are Layer 4, IP addresses and routers are Layer 3, MAC addresses and switches are Layer 2, and cables and hubs are Layer 1.

studyNotes.heading: The TCP IP model and encapsulation
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will compare the second model you must know, and then follow a web request down through the layers, step by step.

The TCP IP model is named after the Transmission Control Protocol and the Internet Protocol. It is the four-layer model the internet really uses. Here is how it lines up with OSI.

- Application: OSI Layers 7, 6 and 5.
- Transport: OSI Layer 4.
- Internet: OSI Layer 3.
- Network Access, also called Link: OSI Layers 2 and 1.

Now for encapsulation. It means each layer wraps the data from above in its own header. A header is a label of control facts. Think of a letter placed in an envelope, the envelope in a mailbag, and the mailbag on a truck. Each wrapper is only for whoever handles that stage.

Here is a worked example of opening a web page.

- Step 1: The top layers create the request. Its name is data.
- Step 2: Transport adds a TCP header with the source and destination ports, such as destination port 443. Its name is a segment. With UDP, it is called a datagram.
- Step 3: Network adds an IP header with the source and destination addresses. Its name is a packet.
- Step 4: Data Link adds a header with MAC addresses, and a trailer called the Frame Check Sequence, which detects errors. Its name is a frame.
- Step 5: Physical sends it as bits.

The receiver reverses these steps, removing the frame wrapper first and the application data last. That is de-encapsulation. Along the way, each router removes the frame and builds a new one for the next link. The IP addresses normally stay the same from end to end, but the MAC addresses change at each hop.

Encapsulation matters for security. A filter that reads only the outer header cannot see what is hidden inside, and this is how attackers smuggle data past controls.

Here is a workplace thought. When a firewall log shows a blocked packet, you know it was judged at Layer 3 or above, not at the cable.

The takeaway is this. Remember four TCP IP layers, and remember data, segment, packet, frame, bits.

studyNotes.heading: TCP and UDP, the two transport choices
studyNotes.body:
Now let us look closely at the two transport protocols, because the exam loves to contrast them.

TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, is connection-oriented. That means the two sides agree to talk before any data moves. TCP numbers every byte, confirms what arrives and resends what is lost. It also slows down when the network is struggling. Think of a registered letter, which someone must sign for.

TCP starts with a three-way handshake, in this exact order.

- SYN, which means synchronize. The client asks to talk and offers a starting number.
- SYN-ACK, which means synchronize-acknowledge. The server agrees, confirms that number and offers its own.
- ACK, which means acknowledge. The client confirms the server's number, and data can begin.

SYN and ACK are flags, which are single on or off switches in the TCP header. Others are FIN, which closes a connection politely, and RST, which is reset and ends it at once. PSH asks for data to be pushed along promptly, and URG marks data as urgent.

UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, is connectionless. It has no handshake, no delivery check and no resending. Think of dropping a postcard in a box and hoping. Its header is only 8 bytes, while a TCP header is at least 20 bytes. So UDP is quicker and lighter.

Which uses which? Web browsing, email and file transfer use TCP, because every byte matters. Live voice, video and most DNS lookups use UDP, because a late piece of sound is useless, and a quick retry is cheaper than a long setup. DNS is the Domain Name System.

There is a security side to this. Because UDP has no handshake, a forged sender address is easy to use, and this helps certain flooding attacks. TCP's handshake makes forging harder, but it creates its own weakness, the SYN flood, which we will study later in this domain.

Here is a workplace example. A call centre finds that its voice calls stutter under load. Moving voice onto TCP would make things worse, because resending old sound only adds delay.

Your takeaway is this. TCP is reliable and starts with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. UDP is fast and makes no promises.

studyNotes.heading: Thinking like a manager about layers
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will turn the model into decisions, because the exam asks what you would advise, and not just what you can recite.

Start with the principle. Every control works at certain layers and cannot see what happens at others. Think of your home. A strong front door does nothing about a thief who climbs in through a window. A burglar alarm does nothing to stop a leaking roof. You need the right protection for each way that harm can arrive.

Here is how controls line up with the layers.

- Layer 1: locked cabinets, protected cable routes, and inspection.
- Layer 2: switch port security, which limits the devices on a port, and network access checks.
- Layers 3 and 4: packet filters, which read addresses and ports, and IPsec.
- Layer 7: web application firewalls and application proxies, which read content.

When a question describes an attack, first name the layer. Next, ask whether the proposed control works at that layer. If it does not, then the option is wrong, however impressive it sounds.

Now a workplace example. A bank is told by an auditor that traffic between two internal systems could be read by anyone on that network segment. The team proposes a bigger firewall at the internet connection. A manager would ask three things. Where is the exposure? It is inside, between the two systems. What is the risk? Readable data in transit. What control fits? Encryption between those systems, such as TLS or IPsec. The firewall sits in the wrong place, so it would not help.

Defense in depth means using controls at several layers, so that the failure of one is not the failure of all. It does not mean buying every product. A manager weighs each control against the value of what it protects and its cost, follows policy, and fixes the cause and not just the symptom.

And always remember that safety comes first. If a network change could affect a hospital's patient monitors, that consideration comes before everything else.

Here is what to take away. Name the layer, choose a control that works there, place it where the risk is, and layer your protections with judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: Open Systems Interconnection: a seven-layer reference map of network communication.
Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol: the four-layer model the internet uses.
Each layer wraps data from the layer above in its own header.
The receiver removes each wrapper, layer by layer.
The TCP data unit at Layer 4.
The data unit at Layer 3. It carries IP addresses.
The data unit at Layer 2. It carries MAC addresses and an error-check trailer.
Media Access Control address: the hardware label of a network card.
How TCP starts a connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

keyPoints: OSI has seven layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.
TCP/IP has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access.
Data units going down are data, segment, packet, frame, bits.
Switches work at Layer 2 and routers work at Layer 3.
Match each security control to the layer where the problem lives.
topics.memoryHook: From Layer 1 up: Please Do Not Take Sweets, Pies, Apples (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).

question.prompt: A school's network team writes a rule that allows or blocks traffic using only IP addresses and port numbers. A manager asks which OSI layers the rule is working at. What is the BEST answer?
options: Layers 1 and 2, because the rule controls how signals reach each device
Layers 2 and 3, because the rule uses hardware addresses and routes
Layers 3 and 4, because IP addresses and ports belong to those layers
Layers 6 and 7, because the rule understands what each program is sending
question.explanation: IP addresses belong to Layer 3 and port numbers belong to Layer 4. Layers 2 and 3 is tempting, but Layer 2 uses MAC addresses, and the rule does not read those.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Users report that they can reach an internal server by typing its IP address, but not by typing its name. Which OSI layer is the MOST likely home of the failing service?
options: Layer 7, because name lookup is an application service
Layer 3, because the server's address cannot be routed at all
Layer 2, because hardware addresses have stopped being resolved
Layer 1, because the signal on the cable has become too weak
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reaching the server by IP address shows Layers 1 to 3 are working. The Domain Name System is a Layer 7 service. Layer 3 is tempting, but the working IP address rules out a routing failure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A trainer asks a new analyst to state the data unit names as a web request travels down the stack on the sending computer. Which sequence is the MOST accurate?
options: Data, packet, segment, frame, bits
Data, frame, packet, segment, bits
Data, segment, packet, frame, bits
Bits, frame, packet, segment, data
practiceQuestions.explanation: Going down, the names are data, segment, packet, frame and bits. The last option is tempting, but that is the order on the receiving side, going up.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a walk-through, an auditor finds that network cable runs pass through an unlocked ceiling space used by contractors. Which action BEST addresses the layer at which this exposure exists?
options: Turn on stricter address filtering at each network router
Secure the cable route and inspect it on a regular schedule
Add a web application firewall to the main company website
Require longer and more complex passwords from every contractor
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exposed cable is a Layer 1 risk, so a physical control fits. Address filtering is tempting, but a device tapped into the cable can listen without any router being involved.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new network device decides where to send traffic by reading destination MAC addresses and learning which port each address sits behind. What is this device MOST likely to be?
options: A router working at the Network layer
A hub repeating signals at the Physical layer
A repeater that boosts signals along a cable
A switch working at the Data Link layer
practiceQuestions.explanation: Switches learn and use MAC addresses at Layer 2. A router is tempting, but routers make decisions using IP addresses at Layer 3.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is designing a live voice service. Sound that arrives late is useless, and small losses are acceptable. Which transport choice is the BEST fit?
options: UDP, because it adds no handshake or resending delay
TCP, because it resends every byte that happens to be lost
ICMP, because it is the protocol that carries status messages
ARP, because it finds the fastest route between the callers
practiceQuestions.explanation: UDP has no handshake and no resending, which suits live sound. TCP is tempting because it is reliable, but resending old sound only adds delay.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An analyst reviews a capture of a new connection. The client sent SYN and the server replied with SYN-ACK. What should the analyst expect to see NEXT in a normal connection?
options: The server sends a FIN to confirm that the connection is open
The client sends an ACK to complete the handshake
The client sends a second SYN carrying its first data bytes
The server sends RST to mark the handshake as complete
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, so the client sends ACK next. RST is tempting as a closing signal, but it aborts a connection and does not complete one.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team documents a control that works at the OSI Presentation layer and must now record it against the four-layer TCP IP model. Where does it BEST belong?
options: The Network Access layer
The Internet layer
The Transport layer
The Application layer
practiceQuestions.explanation: The TCP IP Application layer covers OSI Layers 7, 6 and 5. The Transport layer is tempting because it sits just below, but it matches only OSI Layer 4.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An application converts text into a common character format and compresses it before it is sent across a network. Which OSI layer's function does this MOST closely describe?
options: Session
Transport
Presentation
Data Link
practiceQuestions.explanation: Formatting and compression are Presentation layer functions. Session is tempting because it sits next door, but Session starts, manages and ends conversations.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A receiving computer takes in a frame from its network card and begins processing it. Which wrapper does it remove FIRST?
options: The Data Link header and trailer
The IP header holding the addresses
The TCP header holding the ports
The application's own request header
practiceQuestions.explanation: De-encapsulation works upward, so Layer 2 comes off first. The IP header is tempting because addresses seem to come first, but it sits inside the frame.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Leaders want to spend the entire network security budget on one powerful firewall at the internet connection and drop all other planned controls. What is the BEST advice from the security manager?
options: Agree, because a single stronger device is always simpler to run
Agree, provided that the firewall vendor offers a good warranty
Advise layered controls that are matched to the risks at each level
Advise buying every available product so that no layer is left out
practiceQuestions.explanation: One device cannot see every layer or every path, so controls should match the risks and be weighed against cost. Buying every product is tempting, but defense in depth still requires judgment about value.

topics.name: IP networking and secure protocols
topics.simpleExplanation: Every device on a network needs an address, as every house needs a street number. IP (Internet Protocol) gives those addresses. Ports are the numbered doors into each device. Many older protocols send everything in the open, like a postcard. Secure protocols put the message in a locked box. IPsec protects traffic at the network level. SSH protects remote logins. TLS protects websites. DNS finds addresses, and DNSSEC proves those answers are genuine. You must know what each one protects and what it does not.

studyNotes.heading: IPv4 addresses and a subnet worked example
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at how computers are addressed, starting with the older system that most networks still use.

IP is the Internet Protocol. It gives every device an address, just as every house has a street number. IPv4, which is IP version 4, uses addresses of 32 bits. A bit is a single one or zero. An address is written as four numbers separated by dots, such as 192.168.1.10. That allows about 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough for today's world.

Some ranges are private. They are not routed on the public internet. These are the three to know, and the phrase slash 8 means the first 8 bits name the network.

- 10.0.0.0 slash 8.
- 172.16.0.0 slash 12.
- 192.168.0.0 slash 16.

NAT, which is Network Address Translation, lets many private devices share one public address. Picture one school telephone number with many extensions. NAT saves addresses and hides internal numbering, but it is not a security control by itself.

A subnet is a smaller network cut out of a larger one. Here is a worked example with 192.168.1.0 slash 24.

Slash 24 means 24 bits name the network. An address has 32 bits, so 32 minus 24 leaves 8 bits for devices. Two to the power of 8 is 256. Two addresses are reserved, one for the network itself and one for the broadcast. So 256 minus 2 gives 254 usable addresses.

Try one more. With slash 26, 32 minus 26 leaves 6 bits. Two to the power of 6 is 64. Take away 2, and you have 62 usable addresses.

Here is a workplace example. A company puts its finance computers in their own small subnet. Traffic to and from that subnet must now cross a router or firewall, which gives the security team a place to apply rules and to watch.

Also recognize two special addresses. 127.0.0.1 is the loopback, which means this computer talking to itself. An address starting 169.254 means the computer failed to get an address automatically.

Your takeaway is this. IPv4 is 32 bits, know the three private ranges, and calculate hosts by subtracting from 32.

studyNotes.heading: IPv6, and the four ways to deliver traffic
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the newer address system and at the four ways traffic can be addressed.

IPv6, which is IP version 6, uses addresses of 128 bits. They are written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons. Hexadecimal is counting in base 16, using 0 to 9 and then a to f. A run of zero groups can be shortened once with a double colon, so 2001:db8::1 is a complete address.

IPv6 has no broadcast and no need for NAT, which is Network Address Translation, because addresses are so plentiful. Your device can even build its own address. Instead of ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, it uses Neighbor Discovery. IPv6 was designed with IPsec in mind, but IPsec is not switched on automatically. Do not fall for the claim that IPv6 is encrypted by default.

Here are some special IPv6 addresses. The loopback is written with two colons and a one. Addresses starting fe80 are link-local, which means they work only on the local network segment. Addresses starting ff are multicast.

Now the four ways to deliver traffic. Imagine messages in an office.

- Unicast is one to one. You hand a note to one colleague.
- Broadcast is one to all on the local network. You shout across the room. This exists in IPv4 only.
- Multicast is one to a chosen group. You email only the people who joined a mailing list.
- Anycast is one to the nearest of several servers that share an address. You call a helpline and reach the closest branch.

Now a workplace example of a real risk. Many networks run both IPv4 and IPv6 at once, which is called dual stack. Laptops often have IPv6 switched on by default. If a firewall team writes rules for IPv4 only, the IPv6 path may be wide open. Tunnels that carry IPv6 inside IPv4 can also hide traffic from filters.

A manager's response is to make a deliberate decision. Either secure and monitor IPv6 as carefully as IPv4, or disable it where it is not needed.

Here is what to take away. IPv6 is 128 bits with no broadcast, IPsec is not automatic, and unmonitored IPv6 is a blind spot.

studyNotes.heading: IPsec, AH versus ESP, transport versus tunnel
studyNotes.body:
Now we come to IPsec, one of the most heavily tested topics here. Let us go slowly and be exact.

IPsec stands for IP Security. It protects traffic at Layer 3 of the OSI model, the Open Systems Interconnection map. It has two protection protocols and a key system.

- AH, the Authentication Header, proves origin and integrity. It gives no encryption. Its IP protocol number is 51.
- ESP, the Encapsulating Security Payload, gives encryption, and it can also prove origin and integrity. Its IP protocol number is 50.
- IKE, Internet Key Exchange, agrees the keys and builds Security Associations. It uses UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, on port 500.

A Security Association is a one-way agreement on settings, so a two-way conversation needs two of them.

IPsec has two modes.

- Transport mode protects the payload and keeps the original IP header. It is usually host to host.
- Tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet inside a new one with a new header. It is usually gateway to gateway.

Think of a letter. Transport mode is putting the page in a sealed sleeve, while the envelope still shows who it is for. Tunnel mode is putting the whole envelope inside a new courier bag, addressed from one office to another.

Now combine them.

- AH in transport mode: signs the payload and most of the IP header. Nothing is hidden.
- AH in tunnel mode: signs the whole packet. Nothing is hidden.
- ESP in transport mode: encrypts the payload. The original addresses remain visible.
- ESP in tunnel mode: encrypts the entire original packet. Observers see only the gateway addresses.

One trap is worth knowing. NAT, Network Address Translation, changes the addresses in the IP header. AH protects that header, so NAT breaks AH. ESP does not cover the outer header, and it can pass through NAT by being wrapped in UDP on port 4500.

Here is a workplace example. Two branch offices need a private link across the internet. The gateways use ESP in tunnel mode, so outsiders learn only that the two offices are talking.

The takeaway is this. AH is an autograph, ESP is an envelope, transport keeps the header, and tunnel wraps everything.

studyNotes.heading: SSH and TLS
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at two protocols you meet every day, and at what each one really protects.

SSH, which is Secure Shell, gives you an encrypted remote command line. It runs on port 22. It replaces Telnet and other old tools, which send everything, even passwords, in plain readable text. SSH can also copy files securely. Use SSH version 2, because version 1 had serious flaws.

Think of SSH as a private phone line to a machine, where Telnet is shouting your instructions across a busy car park.

SSH proves the server's identity using a host key. The first time you connect, you are asked to trust that key. Afterwards, a changed key produces a warning. Users should stop and report it, and not just click past it. For logins, public key authentication is stronger than a password. It uses a matched pair of keys, one kept secret and one shared.

TLS, which is Transport Layer Security, protects web traffic and many other applications. HTTPS is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol running over TLS. SSL, the Secure Sockets Layer, was the older parent of TLS, and all versions of SSL are broken and should be retired. TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 are retired too. Use TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

Here is what happens when TLS starts. The client and server agree on settings. The server presents a certificate, which is a digital identity card signed by a trusted authority. The two sides then agree on a shared key for the session. From then on, the data is encrypted and checked for tampering. TLS 1.3 is faster and removes older weak options.

TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and proof of the server's identity. The client is proved only if mutual TLS is used, where both sides show certificates.

Be clear about limits. TLS protects data in transit between two points. It does not protect data stored on the server. It does not stop an attack carried inside a valid connection.

Here is a workplace example. A company's website uses TLS, and it is still breached by an attacker who sends harmful input through the encrypted connection. The lock on the browser only protected the trip.

Your takeaway is this. Replace Telnet with SSH, retire SSL, and remember what TLS does not do.

studyNotes.heading: Port numbers, DNS and DNSSEC
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will learn the port numbers worth memorizing, and then see how names are found and protected.

A port is a numbered door into a computer. Well-known ports run from 0 to 1023. Registered ports run from 1024 to 49151. Dynamic ports run from 49152 to 65535. Here are the ones to know.

- 20 and 21: FTP, the File Transfer Protocol.
- 22: SSH, Secure Shell.
- 23: Telnet.
- 25: SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol.
- 53: DNS, the Domain Name System.
- 67 and 68: DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol.
- 80: HTTP, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
- 88: Kerberos, a ticket-based login.
- 110: POP3, Post Office Protocol version 3.
- 123: NTP, the Network Time Protocol.
- 143: IMAP, the Internet Message Access Protocol.
- 161 and 162: SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol.
- 389: LDAP, the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.
- 443: HTTPS, which is HTTP over Transport Layer Security.
- 445: SMB, Server Message Block, for Windows file sharing.
- 636: LDAPS, which is LDAP over Transport Layer Security.
- 3389: RDP, the Remote Desktop Protocol.

DNS works like a phone book, turning names into addresses. Most lookups use UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, on port 53. Zone transfers, which copy a whole set of records between servers, use TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, on port 53. Large answers also use TCP.

DNSSEC, or DNS Security Extensions, digitally signs records. A resolver can check that an answer came from the right zone and was not changed. So it provides origin proof and integrity. It does not hide your lookups, so it provides no confidentiality. To hide lookups, you use DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS.

A simple way to remember it is this. DNSSEC is a seal on the phone book entry. DNS over HTTPS is a private booth to read the book in.

Here is a workplace example. A company restricts zone transfers to its own secondary servers, because an open transfer hands an attacker a map of the whole network.

Your takeaway is this. Memorize the common ports, and remember that DNSSEC proves answers but does not hide them.

studyNotes.heading: Multilayer and converged protocols
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at two ideas named in the outline: what multilayer protocols imply, and what converged protocols are.

A multilayer protocol works across several layers of the model, and it wraps one protocol inside another. TCP IP is the main example, named for the Transmission Control Protocol and the Internet Protocol. Web traffic is carried inside TCP, inside IP, inside Ethernet. This gives great flexibility. Anything can ride on anything.

That flexibility has a security cost. Think of a parcel inside another parcel. A guard who checks only the outside label never sees the inner one. In the same way, a filter that reads only the outer header can miss what is carried inside.

Attackers use this to create a covert channel, which is a hidden path that moves data in a way that breaks policy. A real example is tunneling stolen data inside DNS lookups, because DNS, the Domain Name System, is usually allowed out through a firewall. Another is VLAN hopping, where VLAN means Virtual Local Area Network, and extra tags are added to a frame to reach a separate virtual network.

The manager's answer is to inspect deeper, restrict what may leave, and watch for odd patterns, such as an unusually large number of lookups from one computer.

Converged protocols carry a kind of traffic that once needed its own separate network over a shared one. The benefit is lower cost and simpler cabling. The risk is that one failure, or one attack, can now affect everything at once.

Here are the examples to recognize.

- InfiniBand over Ethernet: carries high-speed data centre traffic, normally found on special InfiniBand networks, across Ethernet.
- Compute Express Link: a fast connection between processors, memory and accelerators, built on the PCIe link inside a computer. PCIe is Peripheral Component Interconnect Express.
- Fibre Channel over Ethernet: carries storage traffic on Ethernet.
- iSCSI, the Internet Small Computer Systems Interface: carries storage commands over IP networks.
- Voice over IP: carries telephone calls over a data network.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital moves phones and storage onto one network. The savings are real, but a single switch failure could now stop both, so redundancy becomes essential.

Here is what to take away. Wrapping creates hiding places, and convergence creates shared failure.

keyTerms.meaning: Internet Protocol version 6: uses 128-bit addresses and has no broadcast.
Traffic goes to the nearest of several servers sharing one address.
Authentication Header: IPsec part that gives integrity and origin proof, but no encryption.
Encapsulating Security Payload: IPsec part that encrypts.
IPsec mode that wraps the whole original packet in a new one.
IPsec mode that protects only the payload and keeps the original header.
Transport Layer Security: protects application traffic such as web pages.
DNS Security Extensions: signs DNS records for integrity and origin proof, not secrecy.
Carries a special kind of traffic over a shared common network.
A hidden path used to move data in a way that breaks policy.

keyPoints: IPv4 is 32 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits.
AH gives no encryption, while ESP does.
Tunnel mode hides the whole original packet.
DNSSEC proves answers are genuine but does not hide them.
Replace Telnet with SSH, and replace SSL with current TLS.
topics.memoryHook: AH is an Autograph: it proves who signed. ESP is an Envelope: it hides what is inside.

question.prompt: A bank wants customers' computers to be able to prove that answers about the bank's domain name really came from the bank's zone and were not changed on the way. Which step BEST meets this need?
options: Sign the zone with DNSSEC
Move lookups to DNS over HTTPS so that nobody on the path can read them
Allow zone transfers only over TCP port 53
Put the DNS servers on private IP addresses
question.explanation: DNSSEC signs records, so a resolver can check where they came from and that they are unchanged. DNS over HTTPS is tempting, but it protects only the link to the resolver. It hides the lookup and does not prove the record itself is genuine.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A network team must give a new department its own subnet using a slash 26 prefix on an IPv4 network. How many usable host addresses will the department have?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 32 minus 26 leaves 6 bits. Two to the power of 6 is 64, and removing the network and broadcast addresses leaves 62. 64 is tempting, but it counts those two reserved addresses.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organization wants its global DNS service to answer each user from whichever server is closest, while all servers share the same address. Which delivery method BEST describes this design?
options: Unicast, with one fixed path to each individual server
Multicast, with each server joining one chosen group
Broadcast, with one query sent to all servers in the world
Anycast
practiceQuestions.explanation: Anycast sends traffic to the nearest of several servers that share one address. Multicast is tempting, but it delivers to every member of a group and not just to the nearest one.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security review finds that laptops have IPv6 enabled, while firewall rules and monitoring cover only IPv4. What should the security manager recommend?
options: Treat it as low risk, because IPv6 traffic is always encrypted by the protocol itself
Treat it as low risk, because IPv6 has no broadcast traffic that could be misused
Decide whether IPv6 is needed, then either secure and monitor it or disable it
Change every laptop to use a static address until the next network refresh
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unmonitored path is a blind spot, so it needs a deliberate decision. The first option is tempting, but IPsec is not switched on automatically in IPv6.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two servers on the same internal network must exchange data with encryption, and the team wants the IPsec setup with the least overhead for this host-to-host traffic. Which choice is BEST?
options: ESP in transport mode
AH in transport mode
AH in tunnel mode
ESP in tunnel mode between two new gateways
practiceQuestions.explanation: ESP encrypts, and transport mode suits host-to-host traffic without adding a new IP header. ESP in tunnel mode is tempting, but it adds a whole new header and gateways that this need does not call for.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An IPsec connection using only AH keeps failing whenever the traffic passes through a device that performs Network Address Translation. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: AH encrypts the addresses, so the translating device cannot read them
AH covers the IP header, so changing the addresses fails the integrity check
AH works only in tunnel mode, which translation devices do not accept
AH uses TCP port 500, which translation devices always happen to block
practiceQuestions.explanation: AH protects most of the IP header, and address translation changes it, so the check fails. The first option is tempting, but AH does not encrypt anything.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An architect is asked which part of IPsec is responsible for agreeing the keys and setting up the agreed settings between two gateways. What is the BEST answer?
options: The Encapsulating Security Payload
The Authentication Header
Internet Key Exchange
Transport mode
practiceQuestions.explanation: Internet Key Exchange agrees keys and builds Security Associations. The Encapsulating Security Payload is tempting because it uses those keys, but it does not negotiate them.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A scan of a web server shows that it still accepts SSL version 3 and TLS 1.0 alongside TLS 1.2. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Keep all versions so that the widest range of customers can still connect
Keep the old versions, but add a warning notice to the website's front page
Move the old versions to a different port number so that scanners miss them
Disable the old versions and allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3
practiceQuestions.explanation: SSL and TLS 1.0 are retired because of known weaknesses, so the fix is to disable them. Moving them to another port is tempting, but that only hides the weakness and does not remove it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A firewall administrator is asked to permit secure directory lookups from an application to a directory server. Which destination port should the rule MOST likely allow?
practiceQuestions.explanation: LDAP over Transport Layer Security uses port 636. Port 389 is tempting because it is also directory traffic, but that is plain LDAP without encryption.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to stop people on the local coffee shop network from seeing which websites its travelling staff look up. Which option MOST directly meets this requirement?
options: Sign all the company's DNS zones with DNSSEC
Restrict zone transfers to the secondary DNS servers
Send the staff's DNS lookups over HTTPS to a trusted resolver
Move the company's public website to a new set of addresses
practiceQuestions.explanation: DNS over HTTPS encrypts the lookup on its way to the resolver, so nearby observers cannot read it. DNSSEC is tempting, but it proves that answers are genuine and hides nothing.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Monitoring shows one workstation making thousands of DNS lookups for long random-looking names under one domain, even though the workstation's user is on leave. Which explanation is MOST likely?
options: A converged protocol carrying storage traffic over the local Ethernet network
A covert channel moving data out inside DNS traffic
Normal caching behaviour that a busy resolver shows from time to time
A slow network link causing the workstation to retry the same lookup
practiceQuestions.explanation: Encoded names sent to one domain, at volume, suggest data being tunneled through DNS. Retries are tempting, but retries repeat the same name and these names are all different.

topics.name: Wireless and cellular networks
topics.simpleExplanation: Wireless networks send data through the air, so anyone nearby can try to listen. It is like talking in a shop rather than in a closed room. So we must encrypt the data and check who joins. Wi-Fi uses protections called WPA2 and WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access). 802.1X makes every person or device log in. Bluetooth and Zigbee cover short distances. Satellite reaches remote places but can be slow. 4G and 5G mobile networks are stronger, yet you should still protect your own data.

studyNotes.heading: How Wi-Fi works and its standards
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at how Wi-Fi works and at the standards behind it.

A wired network keeps its signal inside a cable. A wireless network sends it through the air, and so it goes through walls and past the car park. Think of the difference between passing a note to a friend and talking aloud in a shop. Anyone nearby can hear the second one. So every wireless design starts from the assumption that others can listen.

Wi-Fi follows the 802.11 family of standards from the IEEE, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. An access point is the box that connects wireless devices to the wired network. The network's name is called the SSID, which is the Service Set Identifier.

Here is the list to recognize. Frequency is measured in gigahertz, and speed in megabits per second.

- 802.11a: 5 gigahertz, up to 54 megabits per second.
- 802.11b: 2.4 gigahertz, up to 11 megabits per second.
- 802.11g: 2.4 gigahertz, up to 54 megabits per second.
- 802.11n, also called Wi-Fi 4: 2.4 and 5 gigahertz, up to 600 megabits per second.
- 802.11ac, or Wi-Fi 5: 5 gigahertz, gigabit speeds.
- 802.11ax, or Wi-Fi 6: 2.4 and 5 gigahertz. Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 gigahertz.
- 802.11be, or Wi-Fi 7: 2.4, 5 and 6 gigahertz.

Lower frequencies reach farther and pass through walls better. Higher frequencies are faster over short distances, but they fade sooner. Think about a neighbour's music, where you hear the deep bass through the wall but not the high notes.

In the 2.4 gigahertz band, channels overlap, and only channels 1, 6 and 11 are normally used side by side without interfering.

Here is a workplace example. A warehouse with thick walls and long aisles may need more access points than expected. A wireless site survey measures where the signal really reaches. It also shows when the signal leaks into the street, where the company does not want it. Antenna type, position and power can then be adjusted.

Here is what to take away. Assume that the air can be heard, know the standards and their bands, and survey the site before you trust the design.

studyNotes.heading: From WEP to WPA3
studyNotes.body:
Now we will follow how Wi-Fi security has improved, because the exam expects you to know exactly what each generation does.

WEP is Wired Equivalent Privacy. It used a cipher called RC4, short for Rivest Cipher 4, with a very short 24-bit starting value, which repeats quickly. Attackers can crack it within minutes. Never use it.

WPA is Wi-Fi Protected Access. The first version added TKIP, the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol. It was a stopgap that still ran on old WEP hardware. Retire it too.

WPA2 uses AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, in a mode called CCMP, the Counter Mode Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol. You only need to remember that CCMP means AES on Wi-Fi. WPA2 protects data well, but its Personal mode has a known weakness. An attacker who records the four-way handshake, which is the login exchange, can take it away and guess the password offline for as long as they like.

WPA3 fixes that. Its Personal mode uses SAE, Simultaneous Authentication of Equals. Each guess requires a live exchange with the network, so offline guessing does not work. SAE also gives forward secrecy, which means that a password stolen later does not unlock traffic that was recorded earlier. WPA3 also requires Protected Management Frames, which stops forged disconnect messages. Its Enterprise mode offers an optional stronger 192-bit setting.

Both WPA2 and WPA3 come in two flavours.

- Personal means one shared password for everyone.
- Enterprise means each person logs in with their own account.

Think of a shared house key compared with a staff card that can be cancelled for one person.

There is a caution about mixed setups. Transition mode lets older WPA2 devices and newer WPA3 devices share a network. An attacker may try to push a device down to the weaker WPA2.

Hiding the network name, and filtering by MAC address, are not real security. MAC stands for Media Access Control and is the hardware label on a network card. Attackers can see and copy both.

Here is a workplace example. A company moving from WPA2-Personal to WPA3-Enterprise gains individual accountability as well as stronger protection.

Your takeaway is this. WEP and TKIP are finished, WPA2 means AES, and WPA3 means SAE and no offline guessing.

studyNotes.heading: 802.1X and its three roles
studyNotes.body:
Next we will study 802.1X, which you can say as eight oh two dot one X. It controls who may join a network, and the exam likes its three roles.

802.1X is port-based network access control. It works on Wi-Fi and on wired networks. A port is either closed or open, and until you prove who you are, only login traffic can pass.

Here are the three roles.

- Supplicant: the device asking to join. The visitor.
- Authenticator: the access point or switch. The guard at the gate.
- Authentication server: usually RADIUS, the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. Head office, which says yes or no.

Notice one thing. The guard does not decide. The guard simply passes the request to head office and then acts on the answer.

The login itself is carried by EAP, the Extensible Authentication Protocol. Between the supplicant and the authenticator, EAP travels over the local network. Between the authenticator and the server, EAP is carried inside RADIUS messages.

Here is a worked example of a connection.

- Step 1: A laptop connects. The port is closed to everything but login traffic.
- Step 2: The access point asks the laptop to identify itself.
- Step 3: The laptop answers, and the access point relays this to the RADIUS server.
- Step 4: The server and laptop complete an EAP method, and the server decides.
- Step 5: The server tells the access point to accept or reject, and if accepted, the port opens.

EAP has several methods.

- EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides. TLS is Transport Layer Security. This is the strongest common choice.
- PEAP, Protected EAP, builds a protected tunnel with a server certificate, and then checks a password inside it.
- EAP-TTLS, Tunneled TLS, is similar.
- LEAP, Lightweight EAP, is old and broken. Avoid it.

One common error is letting devices connect without checking the server's certificate. A fake access point can then collect logins.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital uses EAP-TLS, so staff devices need a certificate that the hospital issued. A stolen password alone will not get anyone on.

The takeaway is this. Supplicant asks, authenticator relays and enforces, and the authentication server decides.

studyNotes.heading: Wireless attacks and how a manager responds
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at how wireless networks are attacked, and at what a sensible organization does about it.

Here are the attacks to recognize. A rogue access point is an unauthorized one that is connected to your network, often placed there innocently by staff who wanted better coverage. An evil twin is a fake access point that imitates your network's name, so that devices connect to it. A deauthentication attack sends forged messages that disconnect users, often to force them to reconnect to an evil twin. Jamming floods the radio band with noise and so denies service. War driving means travelling around to map wireless networks.

Think of a fake bank branch set up down the road, with the same logo over the door. Customers walk in and hand over their details, because everything looks normal.

Here are the controls, matched to those attacks.

For rogue access points and evil twins, use a wireless intrusion prevention system, which watches the airwaves for devices that should not be there. Use 802.1X, which is port-based access control, so that a rogue device plugged into the wall cannot connect. Require devices to check the server's certificate, so that an evil twin is exposed.

For deauthentication, use Protected Management Frames, which are required under WPA3, or Wi-Fi Protected Access version 3.

For jamming, remember that it is a physical problem. Encryption cannot help, so have a wired fallback for critical services.

A captive portal, the web page you see in hotels, is not encryption. It only controls who gets online. WPS, or Wi-Fi Protected Setup, has a weak number code that can be guessed, so turn it off.

Guest networks should be separate from business networks. Think of a shop's customer area, kept apart from the stockroom.

Here is a workplace example. A manager finds an unapproved access point under a desk in the sales office. The technical response is to remove it. The manager's response goes further and asks why. If staff had poor coverage, then the cause must be fixed, or the next one will soon appear. Policy should also be repeated to staff.

Here is what to take away. Know the attacks by name, match each to a control, and fix the reason that staff worked around security.

studyNotes.heading: Bluetooth and Zigbee
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at two short-range technologies, each with its own weak points.

Bluetooth links nearby devices on the 2.4 gigahertz band, using frequency hopping, which means it jumps quickly between many channels. It is designed for short range, usually up to around ten metres for common devices, but an attacker with a strong antenna can reach further. So distance alone is not a defence.

Pairing is when two Bluetooth devices agree to trust each other. Older pairing methods were weak. Modern Secure Simple Pairing is better, particularly when the user compares a number on both screens.

Here are three attacks to learn as a set.

- Bluejacking: sending unwanted messages to a nearby device. It is annoying, but it takes no data.
- Bluesnarfing: stealing data, such as contacts and messages.
- Bluebugging: taking control of the device, so that an attacker could make calls or listen in.

A simple way to remember them is this. Jacking is a nuisance, snarfing is a theft, and bugging is a takeover.

Defences are mostly habits. Turn Bluetooth off when you are not using it. Keep the device non-discoverable. Pair only in private places. Apply patches. Think of a front door. Leaving it open with a sign saying that you are home is not sensible, even in a quiet street.

Here is a workplace example. A company policy bans Bluetooth file transfer on phones used for sensitive work, and mobile device management enforces that setting. Mobile device management is central software that controls phones and tablets.

Zigbee follows the standard IEEE 802.15.4, where IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. It is a low-power, low-speed wireless mesh, which means each device can pass messages on for its neighbours. It suits sensors and smart buildings, because batteries last for years and the network can cover a large space.

Zigbee can use 128-bit encryption with AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard. Its weakness is often in key handling, such as a key shared across many devices or sent during joining.

Imagine a building where lights, door sensors and air conditioning all use a mesh. If an attacker can join it, the damage may be wide. So keep these devices on a separate network from business systems.

Here is your takeaway. Short range is not a security control, so patch, limit pairing and isolate.

studyNotes.heading: Satellite and cellular networks
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will look at the two wide-area wireless technologies in the outline, satellite and cellular.

Satellite reaches places with no cables, such as ships, mines and remote villages. There are three orbits to know.

- GEO, geostationary orbit, is about 36,000 kilometres up. The satellite seems to stay still in the sky. A round trip takes about 600 milliseconds.
- MEO, medium Earth orbit, is in between.
- LEO, low Earth orbit, is usually under 2,000 kilometres up, with a delay of tens of milliseconds. Many small satellites are needed, because each one is only overhead for minutes.

Think of shouting across a canyon compared with talking across a table. Distance creates delay, and voice calls suffer the most from it.

A satellite beam covers a very wide area, so anyone within the beam may be able to receive the signal. Treat the link as public, and encrypt the traffic yourself. Weather can also weaken the signal. A satellite provider is also a third party, whose security you must assess.

Cellular networks divide land into cells, each served by a tower. 4G is the fourth generation of mobile networks and commonly means LTE, or Long-Term Evolution. 5G is the fifth generation. It brings higher speed, lower delay and network slicing, which creates separate virtual networks on shared equipment. So a utility company might have its own slice for meters.

5G improves security in two ways. It conceals the permanent subscriber identity, so listeners cannot easily track a phone. And it has stronger mutual authentication, where the phone and the network each prove themselves. Very high 5G frequencies have short range, so more small cells are needed.

Here is the key point. Radio encryption covers only the link from phone to tower. Beyond that, your data crosses the carrier's network. Fake towers can also trick phones, and forced downgrades can push them onto older, weaker networks.

Here is a workplace example. Field engineers send customer data from phones. The manager does not rely on the mobile carrier alone. Data is protected end to end using TLS, which is Transport Layer Security, or a VPN, which is a Virtual Private Network.

Your takeaway is this. Treat satellite and cellular links as untrusted, and protect your data from end to end.

keyTerms.meaning: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3: current Wi-Fi security that resists offline password guessing.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: the WPA3 Personal login exchange.
Port-based access control that makes a device log in before joining.
In 802.1X, the device asking to join.
In 802.1X, the switch or access point that controls entry.
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service: a central login check server.
Stealing data from a device over Bluetooth.
A low-power, low-speed wireless mesh for sensors.
A 5G feature that creates separate virtual networks on shared equipment.

keyPoints: Use WPA3, or WPA2 with AES where WPA3 is not possible.
802.1X roles are supplicant, authenticator and authentication server.
Hidden network names and MAC filters are not real security.
Cellular radio encryption stops at the tower, so protect data end to end.
topics.memoryHook: Visitor, Guard, Head Office: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server.

question.prompt: An office Wi-Fi network uses one shared password. Staff leave often, and auditors say the company cannot tell who connected. Which change BEST solves the problem?
options: Move to WPA3-Personal with a much longer shared passphrase
Hide the network name and allow only approved MAC addresses
Keep WPA2-Personal and change the shared passphrase every time someone leaves the company
Use WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and a RADIUS server
question.explanation: Enterprise mode with 802.1X gives each person their own login, so access can be traced and removed one person at a time. A longer shared passphrase is tempting, but everyone still shares it, so the auditors' problem remains.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A coffee shop owner wants customers to stop being able to record the Wi-Fi login exchange and then guess the shared password at home. Which change MOST directly addresses this?
options: Hide the network name so that the login exchange cannot be seen
Move from WPA2-Personal to WPA3-Personal
Change the router to the 5 gigahertz band instead of 2.4 gigahertz
Require customers to accept the terms on a captive portal page
practiceQuestions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE, so every guess needs a live exchange and offline guessing fails. A captive portal is tempting, but it only controls who gets online and does not change the login exchange.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During an 802.1X rollout, a colleague asks which component actually decides whether a user may join the network. What is the BEST answer?
options: The supplicant running on the user's laptop
The access point acting as the authenticator
The switch port that carries the user's traffic
The authentication server, usually RADIUS
practiceQuestions.explanation: The authentication server makes the decision. The access point is tempting because it enforces the result, but it only relays the request and acts on the answer.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A university wants the strongest common method of 802.1X login, and it can issue certificates to all its managed devices. Which method is the BEST choice?
options: EAP-TLS
PEAP with an individual username and a password
LEAP
A single shared password in Personal mode
practiceQuestions.explanation: EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides and is the strongest common method. PEAP is tempting and is reasonable, but it still relies on a password that can be stolen.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Staff complain of being disconnected from Wi-Fi repeatedly. An analyst then sees an access point with the company's network name on a channel the company does not use. What is this MOST likely to be?
options: Bluesnarfing aimed at the company's staff phones
A jamming attack on all the 5 gigahertz channels
A deauthentication attack that supports an evil twin
War driving carried out from the company's car park
practiceQuestions.explanation: Forced disconnects combined with a look-alike network suggest an evil twin. Jamming is tempting, but jamming does not create a look-alike access point.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager finds that a sales team installed its own access point because the office has poor coverage. After the device is removed, what is the BEST next step?
options: Discipline the whole team and consider the matter closed
Hide the name of the official network so that it is harder to find
Purchase a stronger signal jammer for that office
Fix the coverage problem through the approved process and remind staff of policy
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fixing the cause stops the next rogue device from appearing. Discipline is tempting, but it leaves staff with the same coverage problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee's phone was found to have had its contact list copied by someone nearby over Bluetooth, without any pairing request being accepted. Which attack BEST matches this?
options: Bluejacking
Bluebugging
Bluesnarfing
Jamming
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stealing data over Bluetooth is bluesnarfing. Bluejacking is tempting because of the similar name, but it only sends unwanted messages.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A smart building uses a low-power wireless mesh for its door sensors and lighting. Which step gives the BEST reduction in risk to the company's business systems?
options: Place the mesh devices on a network separated from business systems
Raise the transmit power of each sensor so that signals stay strong
Replace the battery in every sensor on a regular yearly schedule
Rename the mesh network so that its purpose is less obvious to visitors
practiceQuestions.explanation: Separation limits what a compromised sensor can reach. Renaming is tempting because it seems to hide the network, but hiding a name is not real security.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A shipping company must connect a remote vessel, and voice quality is a priority. Which option is MOST likely to give the lowest delay?
options: A geostationary satellite service with a larger dish antenna
A low Earth orbit satellite service
A geostationary service with higher monthly data limits
Any satellite service, since all orbits have the same delay
practiceQuestions.explanation: Low Earth orbit satellites are far closer, so the delay is tens of milliseconds. A larger dish is tempting, but it improves the signal and cannot shorten the distance of about 36,000 kilometres.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A city utility wants smart meter traffic kept logically apart from public traffic on a mobile carrier's shared equipment. Which 5G feature BEST meets this need?
options: Short-range small cells
Concealed subscriber identity
Network slicing
Mutual authentication
practiceQuestions.explanation: Network slicing creates separate virtual networks on shared equipment. Concealed subscriber identity is tempting because it adds privacy, but it does not separate any traffic.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security team is told that sensitive data is safe because the company's phones use 5G radio encryption. What is the BEST response from the security manager?
options: Agree, because 5G radio encryption protects data the whole way to its destination
Agree, because a carrier's own network can always be fully trusted
Ask for the phones to be moved to 4G, which offers far stronger end-to-end encryption
Point out that radio encryption stops at the carrier, so data needs end-to-end protection
practiceQuestions.explanation: Radio encryption covers only the phone to tower link, so end-to-end protection is still needed. The first option is tempting, but the carrier's network lies beyond the part that the radio encryption protects.

topics.name: Segmentation and modern network design
topics.simpleExplanation: A ship has separate compartments so one leak does not sink it. Networks work the same way. Segmentation splits a network into zones, so an intruder in one zone cannot reach everything. A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) does this in switches. Microsegmentation goes further and walls off single servers. SDN (Software-Defined Networking) lets software run the network from one place. You should also know the direction traffic flows and how to measure whether the network is healthy.

studyNotes.heading: Physical segmentation
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at why networks are split into zones, and then at the physical way of doing it.

A ship is built with separate compartments, so that one leak does not sink it. A network follows the same thinking. Segmentation means dividing a network into zones, so an intruder who gets into one zone cannot simply reach everything. It also keeps failures contained and helps performance.

Physical segmentation uses separate equipment. Different cables and different switches carry different traffic. The outline names three ideas here, so let us take each in turn.

In-band management means that the people managing a device reach it through the same network that carries ordinary traffic. It is cheap and simple. Its weakness is plain. If that network fails, or is under attack, then you lose your way in just when you need it most.

Out-of-band management means there is a separate path, used only for management. It may be a dedicated network or a console connection. Think of a building with a separate service staircase. Even if the main staircase is blocked, the maintenance team can still get to every floor. Out-of-band management also keeps administrator traffic away from ordinary users.

An air gap means no network connection at all between two systems. Think of a filing cabinet in a locked room with no telephone. Nothing reaches it except by someone walking in. Air-gapped systems are used for things like weapons systems, some industrial controls and highly classified data.

An air gap is strong, but it is not perfect. Data still has to move in and out, often on removable media such as a USB drive. USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. If a contractor brings an infected drive across the gap, then the gap has been crossed. So an air gap needs strict controls on media, and people need to follow them.

Here is a workplace example. A power company keeps its plant control systems physically separate from office computers. When a virus spreads through the office, the plant keeps running. The cost of duplicate equipment was justified by the harm of an outage, including harm to the public.

Here is what to take away. Segmentation limits damage, in-band shares the road, out-of-band has its own road, and an air gap has no road at all.

studyNotes.heading: Logical segmentation
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at logical segmentation, where equipment is shared and software keeps the traffic apart.

Imagine one large office where the desks are colour-coded, and people may only talk to those with the same colour. The room is the same. The separation is created by rules. Logical segmentation works just like this, and it is cheaper and more flexible than buying separate hardware.

The outline names four kinds.

A VLAN is a Virtual Local Area Network. It separates traffic inside switches, using a tag defined in the standard 802.1Q. The tag carries a number that says which VLAN a frame belongs to. Devices in different VLANs cannot talk unless a router or Layer 3 device passes traffic between them.

VLANs have a known weakness called VLAN hopping. In switch spoofing, a computer pretends to be a switch so that it can see all the VLANs. In double tagging, an attacker adds two tags to a frame, and the second one carries it into another VLAN. To defend, turn off automatic trunking, change the native VLAN to an unused one, and do not trust a VLAN alone for strong separation. A trunk is a link that carries several VLANs at once.

A VPN is a Virtual Private Network. It creates an encrypted path across a shared network, such as the internet.

VRF is Virtual Routing and Forwarding. It keeps separate routing tables inside one router, so that traffic in one table cannot see another. Two customers can even use the same internal addresses without conflict.

A virtual domain divides one physical firewall into several separate virtual firewalls, each with its own rules and administrators.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital uses VLANs to separate medical devices from guest Wi-Fi, and places a firewall between the VLANs. The VLAN keeps the traffic apart, and the firewall decides what may cross. A manager should know that both are needed.

One caution remains. Logical separation depends on correct configuration. A single wrong change can join two zones without anyone noticing. So configuration needs change control and regular review.

The takeaway is this. VLANs separate traffic inside switches, VRF separates routing, a virtual domain separates a firewall, and all of them depend on careful configuration.

studyNotes.heading: Microsegmentation and overlays
studyNotes.body:
Next we will see how segmentation can go right down to a single workload, and what makes that possible.

Ordinary segmentation is like having separate floors in a building. Microsegmentation is like putting a lock on every room, and checking your pass at every door. Even if you get onto the floor, you cannot go into each room.

In technical terms, microsegmentation sets security rules around each workload. A workload is a server, a virtual machine or a container. It uses distributed firewalls, distributed routers and distributed IDS or IPS. IDS is an intrusion detection system, which raises an alert, and IPS is an intrusion prevention system, which can block. The word distributed means that enforcement runs close to each workload, rather than in one central box.

It supports zero trust, an approach in which nothing is trusted just because of where it sits on the network. Each request has to be checked every time.

How can a rule follow a workload that moves around a data centre? This is where overlay networks come in. An overlay is a virtual network running on top of a physical one by using encapsulation. Encapsulation means wrapping one piece of traffic inside another. The physical network, called the underlay, only sees the outer wrapper.

The main example is VXLAN, or Virtual Extensible LAN, where LAN means Local Area Network. It wraps Layer 2 frames inside UDP packets, normally on port 4789. UDP is the User Datagram Protocol.

Here is a worked example of why this matters. A VLAN, or Virtual Local Area Network, has an ID of 12 bits. Two to the power of 12 is 4,096 values, and two of these are reserved, leaving 4,094 usable. A VXLAN has an ID of 24 bits. Two to the power of 24 is 16,777,216, or about 16 million segments. A large cloud provider with many customers needs that second number.

There is one caution. Overlays carry traffic inside wrappers, so a monitoring tool on the underlay may not see inside. Monitoring must understand the overlay.

Here is a workplace example. A bank writes rules allowing its web servers to reach only one application server. If a web server is compromised, the intruder cannot reach the rest of the data centre.

Here is your takeaway. Microsegmentation puts a lock on every room, overlays make that portable, and zero trust is the mindset behind it.

studyNotes.heading: Planes, software-defined networks and cloud
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how modern networks are run by software, starting with three words you must know.

Every network device does three kinds of work, called planes.

- Data plane: moves the traffic. It is also called the forwarding plane.
- Control plane: decides where traffic should go.
- Management plane: where staff configure and monitor.

Think of an airport. The planes on the runway and in the air are the data plane. The control tower directing them is the control plane. The airport office that sets the schedules and rosters is the management plane.

SDN, which is Software-Defined Networking, separates the control plane from the data plane. A central controller makes decisions, and the switches simply follow them. The controller is reached through APIs, or Application Programming Interfaces, which are agreed ways for software to talk to software. Applications use northbound APIs to talk to the controller. The controller uses southbound APIs to talk to switches.

SDN brings speed and consistency, because one change can reach hundreds of devices. That is also the danger. A compromised controller can change everything. So protect it with strong access control, a separate management network, and logging.

NFV, which is Network Functions Virtualization, runs firewalls, routers and similar functions as software on ordinary servers rather than as dedicated boxes.

SD-WAN, or Software-Defined Wide Area Network, steers branch office traffic across several links according to policy. A voice call might take the best quality link, while a backup job uses the cheapest one.

A VPC, or Virtual Private Cloud, is your own logically isolated network inside a public cloud. You choose the address ranges, subnets and routes. Security groups act as firewall rules around resources. Remember shared responsibility. The cloud provider secures the underlying platform, while you secure your configuration. A storage service left open to the world is the customer's error.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer opens fifty new shops and uses SD-WAN to apply one security policy to all of them from a central console. Before going live, the security manager insists that administrator access to that console requires multi-factor authentication, which means more than one kind of proof.

Your takeaway is this. Data moves, control decides, and management configures. SDN centralizes the control, so protect the controller.

studyNotes.heading: Traffic flows, edge networks and content delivery
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at the directions in which traffic travels, and what happens at the edge of the network.

North-south traffic enters or leaves the data centre. East-west traffic moves between systems inside it. Picture a hotel. Guests coming through the front door are north-south. Staff walking between rooms along the corridors are east-west.

This matters because a perimeter firewall stands at the front door. It sees north-south traffic, but it often misses east-west traffic altogether. Modern applications have grown much more east-west traffic, and intruders who get in use it to move sideways. That sideways movement is known as lateral movement. It is one of the main reasons for internal segmentation.

Next, the edge network. This is where your network meets the outside world. Three outline words apply.

Ingress means traffic coming in. Egress means traffic going out. Filtering both directions is good practice. Ingress filtering drops incoming packets that claim to come from your own internal addresses, because they must be forged. Egress filtering stops your own systems from sending out packets with forged source addresses, and it can also catch data theft and malware calling home.

Peering means two networks exchange traffic directly with each other, often at an internet exchange point, instead of paying a third network to carry it. It reduces cost and delay. Internet routing between networks uses BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol. BGP trusts what its neighbours say, so a mistake or a false announcement can redirect traffic. Route filtering and checking of route origin reduce this risk.

A CDN, or Content Distribution Network, keeps copies of content close to users. Think of a supermarket chain stocking the most popular goods in every town, rather than making everyone drive to the central warehouse. It speeds up delivery. It also absorbs a lot of attack traffic, because the load is spread over many locations.

There is a trade-off. If the CDN terminates your encrypted connections, it can see your content. It therefore becomes a third party that you must assess under contract.

Here is a workplace example. A media company's site survives a sudden spike in visitors on election night, because a CDN serves the pages from many cities.

Here is what to take away. North-south is the front door, east-west is the corridors, and always filter in both directions at the edge.

studyNotes.heading: Topology, switching, performance and monitoring
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will cover how networks are laid out, how we measure their health, and how we keep watching them.

A topology is the layout of a network. In a star, everything connects to one central device, which is simple but makes a single point of failure. In a ring, each device connects to two neighbours. In a bus, all share a single line. In a mesh, devices have many connections to each other.

Here is a worked example. A full mesh of 5 sites needs 5 times 4, divided by 2 links, which is 10 links. Full meshes are strong but expensive, and the number of links grows quickly.

Switches forward frames in two ways. A cut-through switch forwards after reading the destination, so it is fast but can pass on errors. A store-and-forward switch receives the whole frame and checks it first, so it is slower but cleaner.

Now the performance measures.

- Bandwidth: the most that a link can carry.
- Throughput: what it really carries.
- Latency: delay.
- Jitter: variation in delay.
- Signal-to-noise ratio: signal strength compared with background noise.

Think of a motorway. Bandwidth is the number of lanes, throughput is the number of cars that really get through, latency is how long the journey takes, and jitter is when the same journey takes ten minutes one day and forty the next.

Here is a worked example. A 1,000 megabit link delivers 700 megabits in testing. Throughput is 700 divided by 1,000, which is 70 percent of bandwidth. Jitter is what ruins voice and video, even when latency looks fine on average.

Lastly, monitoring and management. Network observability means being able to understand what the network is doing from its logs, metrics and flow records. Traffic flow analysis shows who talks to whom. Traffic shaping controls the pace of traffic, so that important services get priority. Capacity management plans for growth before links fill up. Fault detection and handling finds failures and restores service, often automatically.

Here is a workplace example. Flow records show one server sending large amounts of data to another country at night. Without observability, nobody would have noticed.

Your takeaway is this. Bandwidth is capacity, throughput is delivery, jitter is uneven delay, and you cannot protect what you cannot see.

keyTerms.meaning: Virtual Local Area Network: logical separation of traffic inside switches.
Virtual Routing and Forwarding: separate routing tables in one router.
Security rules set around each individual workload.
Virtual Extensible LAN: carries Layer 2 frames inside UDP across a network, with about 16 million IDs.
Software-Defined Networking: separates the control plane from the data plane.
Software-Defined Wide Area Network: policy-based steering across wide area links.
