Spoofing means faking an identity. That may be an IP address, where IP is the Internet Protocol. It may be a MAC address, where MAC is Media Access Control, the hardware label on a network card. It may be a caller ID. It is like a person wearing a fake delivery uniform.

Ingress and egress filtering drop packets whose source address cannot be right. Ingress means coming in, and egress means going out.

Now ARP poisoning. ARP is the Address Resolution Protocol, and it links IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network. It has no authentication. Any device can claim anything, and other devices will believe it.

Here is how the attack works.

- Step 1: The attacker sends false replies saying that the gateway's IP address belongs to the attacker's MAC address.
- Step 2: The victims update their tables.
- Step 3: Traffic meant for the gateway now flows through the attacker.
- Step 4: The attacker reads or changes it, and passes it on so that nobody notices.

Think about a neighbour who tells the postman that he has taken over your house number, and then collects all your mail, reads it and puts it back in your box.

The controls are Dynamic ARP Inspection on switches, supported by DHCP snooping. DHCP is the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, which gives out addresses. Snooping records which device received which address. The switch then compares each ARP message with that record. Static entries suit a few critical systems.

Another switch attack is MAC flooding. A switch has a table of addresses, called a content addressable memory table. It learns which device sits on which port. An attacker floods the switch with fake MAC addresses until the table is full. Many switches then send frames out of all ports, so the attacker can listen, as if the switch had become a hub. Port security fixes this by limiting the number of addresses on a port.

Here is a workplace example. Users on one floor begin to see certificate warnings. An analyst finds that the gateway's IP address maps to a desktop computer's MAC address. The pattern points to ARP poisoning.

Your takeaway is this. ARP believes anyone, so switches must check it. And port security limits what a single port can claim.

studyNotes.heading: DNS poisoning
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at attacks on the Domain Name System, which most people trust without thinking about it.

DNS, the Domain Name System, turns names into IP addresses, where IP is the Internet Protocol. It works like a phone book. A resolver is the server that finds answers for you, and it stores them for a while in a cache, which is a short-term store.

DNS poisoning puts false records in that cache. Users then visit a fake site, even though they typed the right name. Think of a phone book with one wrong number printed in it. You dial correctly, you reach the wrong person, and you have no idea anything is wrong.

Here is how the classic attack works.

- Step 1: The attacker makes a resolver ask about a name.
- Step 2: While the resolver is waiting, the attacker sends forged replies.
- Step 3: If a forged reply matches the request's details and arrives first, the resolver accepts it.
- Step 4: The false record is cached and served to everybody using that resolver, until it expires.

This is why DNS uses random query IDs and random source ports. An attacker has to guess both. A query ID has 16 bits, which gives 65,536 possible values. Adding a random port makes guessing far harder.

Here are the controls.

- DNSSEC, or DNS Security Extensions, signs records so that forged answers can be detected.
- Random query ports and IDs.
- Patched and restricted resolvers, which only answer your own users.

Do not confuse this with some similar sounding attacks. DNS hijacking means changing the real settings, such as at the domain registrar. Pharming is the general term for sending users to a fake site through false name resolution. A hosts file on a computer can also be altered, which overrides DNS for that machine.

Certificates help here too. If a user reaches a fake site, the site will not normally be able to show a valid certificate for the real name, and the browser will warn them. That is why users must not ignore those warnings.

Here is a workplace example. A company's staff are sent to a fake login page although the address looks right. The team traces this to a poisoned resolver.

Here is what to take away. Poisoning corrupts the phone book, and DNSSEC lets you check the entry.

studyNotes.heading: On-path attacks, sniffing and session hijacking
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at attacks where someone gets into the middle of a conversation, or simply listens to it.

An on-path attack, once called man-in-the-middle, places the attacker between two parties, in order to read or change traffic. Both sides believe that they are talking directly to each other. Imagine a translator who secretly changes what is said in both directions. Rogue access points and ARP poisoning often set this up. ARP is the Address Resolution Protocol.

The controls are TLS, or Transport Layer Security, with proper certificate checks, VPNs or Virtual Private Networks, and mutual authentication, where both sides prove who they are. Train users not to ignore certificate warnings, because a warning is often the only visible sign of an on-path attack.

There is also SSL stripping, where the attacker quietly downgrades a connection to unencrypted HTTP, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. SSL is the Secure Sockets Layer, the older name for this protection. HSTS, or HTTP Strict Transport Security, tells browsers to use only encrypted connections for a site.

Sniffing means capturing traffic. It is passive, and hard to detect, because the attacker sends nothing. Encryption is the main control. Also use switches rather than hubs, enable port security and restrict mirror ports. A mirror port copies traffic for analysis, so it should only be used by those who are authorized.

Think of the difference between someone overhearing your phone call on a train and someone who has picked up an extension in your house. Both are listening. One is a matter of luck, and the other is an intrusion.

Session hijacking is when an attacker takes over a connection that has already been authenticated, frequently by stealing a session token, which is a value that identifies you after you log in. Protect tokens with TLS, make them expire, and use random values.

A replay attack captures valid traffic and sends it again later. Think of someone recording the sound of your garage door remote and playing it back. Controls include timestamps, sequence numbers and values that are used only once.

Here is a workplace example. A traveller joins a fake hotel Wi-Fi network. Since the company uses a VPN and enforces TLS, the attacker on the path sees only scrambled data.

Your takeaway is this. Encryption defeats listening, and strong authentication and certificate checks expose the person in the middle.

studyNotes.heading: Thinking like a manager about attacks
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will pull the attacks together, and practise the thinking that the exam rewards.

The method has three steps. First, name the attack from the symptoms. Second, identify the layer or service affected. Third, choose the control that fixes the cause.

Think about going to the doctor. A good doctor does not prescribe anything until they have worked out what is wrong. In the same way, a security adviser names the problem first.

Here is a list of symptoms and what they usually mean.

- Internet link is completely full: volumetric DDoS, which is distributed denial of service. Clean it upstream.
- Many half-open connections, link not full: SYN flood. Use SYN cookies.
- Gateway's address mapped to an ordinary computer: ARP poisoning. Use Dynamic ARP Inspection.
- Correct name leads to a fake site: DNS poisoning. Use DNSSEC. DNS is the Domain Name System, and DNSSEC is its security extensions.
- Sudden certificate warnings: on-path attack. Investigate, do not click through.
- Traffic read without any sign: sniffing. Encrypt it.

Notice how a well-chosen control is specific. A web application firewall, however good, does nothing for an ARP problem. An exam option can be a real and useful security control and still be the wrong answer, because it does not fix this particular problem.

Now the manager's actions. An attack in progress is an incident, so follow the incident response plan. Do not improvise. Contain the damage first. Protect people's safety before anything else. Tell management, using the agreed reporting path. Preserve evidence if the case could go to law. Then find and remove the root cause, and capture the lessons learned so that it does not happen again.

Do not attack back. Striking the attacker's systems is usually illegal, and they may belong to an innocent victim of a botnet.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital's website is flooded during a public health emergency. The first concern is that patients can reach critical services, so the team activates the agreed scrubbing service, informs leaders, and communicates to the public. Only afterwards do they perform a detailed review and strengthen the design.

Here is what to take away. Name the attack, fix the cause, follow the plan, tell management, and never hit back. Above all, remember that people's safety always comes first.

keyTerms.meaning: Distributed denial of service: flooding a target from many machines at once.
A group of infected computers under an attacker's control.
A small request causes a much larger reply aimed at the victim.
Filling a server with half-open TCP connections.
A method that saves no connection state until the handshake finishes.
False Address Resolution Protocol replies that redirect local traffic.
A switch feature that checks ARP messages against a trusted table.
Placing false records in a DNS cache.
An attacker sits between two parties to read or change traffic.
Capturing network traffic to read it.

keyPoints: A full internet link must be cleaned upstream, not at your own firewall.
SYN cookies defend against SYN floods.
Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping stops ARP poisoning.
DNSSEC defends against forged DNS records.
Encryption is the main control against sniffing and on-path attacks.
topics.memoryHook: Block, Pretend, Listen: flood attacks block, spoofing pretends, sniffing listens.

question.prompt: A company web server shows thousands of connections stuck in a half-open state, and real customers are being refused. The internet link is not full. Which control BEST addresses this attack?
options: Sign the company's DNS zone with DNSSEC so that customers reach the real server
Enable SYN cookies on the server or edge device
Keep web server logs for a longer period so that the attack can be studied
Add static ARP entries on the web server for the local gateway
question.explanation: Half-open connections are the sign of a SYN flood, and SYN cookies stop the table from filling. DNSSEC is tempting because it is a good control, but it protects name records and does nothing about TCP handshakes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker sends small queries with a forged sender address to many public DNS servers, and each server sends a much larger answer to the victim. Which description BEST fits this attack?
options: A SYN flood against the DNS servers
A reflection attack with amplification
DNS poisoning of a resolver's cache
A session hijack of a DNS transaction
practiceQuestions.explanation: Forged replies aimed at the victim are reflection, and larger replies are amplification. DNS poisoning is tempting because DNS is involved, but no false records are being stored.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker's query of 50 bytes produces a reply of 2,500 bytes. If the attacker sends 2 megabits per second of these queries, how much traffic reaches the victim?
options: 52 megabits per second
1,250 megabits per second
25 megabits per second
100 megabits per second
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2,500 divided by 50 gives an amplification of 50, and 2 times 50 is 100 megabits per second. 52 is tempting, but amplification multiplies and does not add.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An analyst captures ping requests sent to a network's broadcast address, all showing a single company's server as the sender. Which attack is the MOST likely?
options: Smurf
Teardrop
ARP poisoning
Replay
practiceQuestions.explanation: A smurf attack sends ping requests to a broadcast address with the victim's address forged. Teardrop is tempting as another older attack, but it sends overlapping fragments.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A web server's table of half-open connections keeps filling, even at a low traffic volume. What is happening in the TCP handshake that makes this attack succeed?
options: The server never sends SYN-ACK in response to the client's request
The client sends ACK first, and the server cannot process it in order
The final ACK never arrives while the server holds resources
The server sends FIN straight after receiving each SYN packet
practiceQuestions.explanation: The attacker sends SYN and never completes the handshake, so the server waits with memory reserved. The first option is tempting, but the server does send SYN-ACK, and that is what ties up its resources.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A server can hold 2,000 half-open connections, each for 50 seconds. About how many forged SYN packets per second are enough to keep the table full?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2,000 divided by 50 is 40 packets per second. 100,000 is tempting if you multiply instead of divide, but the table only needs to be refilled as entries time out.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A switch is flooded with thousands of fake source MAC addresses, and an attacker then sees traffic intended for other devices. Which control BEST prevents this?
options: Signing the company's DNS zones with DNSSEC
Configuring port security to limit addresses on a port
Moving the internet link to a different provider
Longer certificate lifetimes for internal web servers
practiceQuestions.explanation: MAC flooding fills the switch's table, and port security limits the addresses that a port can claim. DNSSEC is tempting as a good control, but it deals with name records and not with switch tables.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Users reach a fake banking page although they typed the correct address, and a cached record on the company's resolver points to an unknown server. What is the BEST immediate technical step in the response plan?
options: Flush the poisoned cache and restrict the resolver
Ask each user to retype the bank's address more carefully
Increase the size of the resolver's memory for caching
Add a Dynamic ARP Inspection rule on every access switch
practiceQuestions.explanation: The evidence points to DNS poisoning, so the false record must be removed and the resolver restricted. Dynamic ARP Inspection is tempting as a local network control, but the fault is in the DNS cache.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker captures an encrypted login message from a remote door controller, and later sends the same message again to open the door. Which control BEST prevents this?
options: A longer encryption key used for the door controller message
A larger bandwidth link to the door controller's location
A sign on the door saying that access is being monitored
A value that is used once and rejected if it is sent again
practiceQuestions.explanation: A replay reuses valid traffic, so a value used only once makes the copy useless. A longer key is tempting, but the attacker does not need to break the encryption to resend the message.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A traveller's browser is quietly served an unencrypted version of a company login page by someone on the same public network. Which control BEST prevents this type of downgrade?
options: A longer password policy across the company
A larger proxy server cache for the login page
HSTS, so that browsers insist on an encrypted connection
A new DNS name for the company login page
practiceQuestions.explanation: HTTP Strict Transport Security tells browsers to use only encrypted connections. A longer password is tempting, but the attacker would simply capture it from the unencrypted page.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a major attack on a company's website, a senior leader tells the security manager to launch a counterattack against the addresses involved. What is the BEST response?
options: Launch the counterattack, but only outside of business hours
Decline, follow the response plan, and contact the upstream provider
Launch the counterattack against half the addresses as a test
Decline, and shut down all of the company's internet connections
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hitting back is usually illegal, and those addresses may belong to innocent victims of a botnet, so the plan should be followed. Shutting down all connections is tempting as a quick stop, but it completes the attacker's goal.

examQuestions.prompt: A security analyst studies a captured unit of network data. It shows a source and destination MAC address, and it ends with an error-check trailer. What is the MOST accurate description of what the analyst is looking at?
options: A packet at the Network layer
A frame at the Data Link layer
A segment at the Transport layer
Bits at the Physical layer
examQuestions.explanation: MAC addresses and an error-check trailer are added at Layer 2, and that data unit is a frame. A packet is tempting, but packets are identified by IP addresses at Layer 3.

examQuestions.prompt: Two company offices connect over the internet. Policy requires that the traffic be encrypted and that outsiders must not see the internal IP addresses of the computers talking. Which IPsec setup BEST meets the policy?
options: AH in transport mode
AH in tunnel mode
ESP in transport mode
ESP in tunnel mode
examQuestions.explanation: ESP encrypts, and tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet, including its internal addresses. ESP in transport mode is tempting, but it leaves the original IP header visible. AH gives no encryption.

examQuestions.prompt: An audit finds that administrators manage network switches using Telnet. The switches can support modern protocols. What should the security manager recommend FIRST to fix the cause of this risk?
options: Replace Telnet with SSH and disable the Telnet service
Move the Telnet service from port 23 to a high, unlisted port number
Require longer and more complex passwords for all Telnet accounts
Add a legal warning banner to every Telnet login screen
examQuestions.explanation: Telnet sends passwords in clear text, so anyone sniffing can read them. SSH removes that cause by encrypting the session. Longer passwords are tempting, but a longer password sent in the clear can still be read.

examQuestions.prompt: Field inspectors send confidential reports from phones over 4G and 5G networks in many regions. Leaders worry about fake cell towers and forced downgrades to older networks. Which action is the BEST protection for the reports?
options: Rely on the radio encryption that the mobile carrier provides
Buy phones with faster 5G radios for all of the inspectors
Use an always-on VPN from each phone to the company
Ask the mobile carrier to raise the data limit on each company phone plan
examQuestions.explanation: A VPN protects the data end to end, whatever radio network carries it. Carrier encryption is tempting, but it protects only the link to the tower and a fake tower or downgrade can weaken it.

examQuestions.prompt: Staff complain that video calls keep breaking up. Monitoring shows the link has plenty of spare capacity and average delay is acceptable, but the delay between packets changes a lot from moment to moment. Which performance measure BEST describes the problem?
options: Bandwidth
Jitter
Signal-to-noise ratio
Throughput
examQuestions.explanation: Jitter is variation in delay, and live voice and video suffer from it. Bandwidth is tempting, but the link has plenty of spare capacity, so capacity is not the issue.

examQuestions.prompt: Contractors at a college plug their own laptops into network sockets in meeting rooms. Some laptops are missing security patches. The college must still let approved contractors work. Which control BEST addresses this?
options: Disable every network socket in every meeting room on the campus
Post a notice asking contractors to patch their laptops before arrival
Add an intrusion detection sensor to watch the meeting room traffic
Deploy NAC that checks device health and quarantines failing devices
examQuestions.explanation: Network access control checks each device before it joins and keeps unhealthy ones away from the main network, while approved users can still work. Disabling all sockets is tempting, but it stops legitimate business.

examQuestions.prompt: A vendor announces that the company's core firewall model will reach end of support next year. The firewall works well today. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Report the risk to management and plan a funded replacement
Keep the firewall in service until it actually fails
Buy a spare unit of the same model and keep it on site for emergencies
Turn off the features of the firewall that depend on vendor updates
examQuestions.explanation: After end of support, new weaknesses will not be fixed, so management needs to know and fund a replacement in time. A spare unit is tempting, but it helps only with hardware failure and does nothing about missing security fixes.

examQuestions.prompt: Policy says all internet traffic from company laptops must pass through the company's web filter, even when staff work from home. Remote staff use a VPN today, but home internet traffic goes straight out. Which change BEST meets the policy?
options: Keep split tunneling and send only the company's own traffic through the VPN
Replace the VPN with L2TP running without IPsec
Configure a full-tunnel VPN for all company laptops
Create a GRE tunnel from each laptop to the head office network
examQuestions.explanation: A full tunnel sends all traffic through the company, where the web filter can inspect it. Split tunneling is what causes the gap today. L2TP without IPsec and GRE provide no encryption.

examQuestions.prompt: Users on one office floor suddenly get certificate warnings. An analyst finds that the gateway's IP address now maps to the MAC address of a desktop computer on that floor. Once the incident is contained, which preventive control is BEST to add on the access switches?
options: DNSSEC signing of the company's internal DNS zones
Longer DHCP lease times for computers on that floor
A perimeter firewall rule blocking outbound UDP port 53
Dynamic ARP Inspection supported by DHCP snooping
examQuestions.explanation: The gateway's IP mapped to a desktop's MAC address shows ARP poisoning, and Dynamic ARP Inspection checks ARP messages against trusted records. DNSSEC is tempting because of the warnings, but this attack is on the local ARP table, not on DNS.

examQuestions.prompt: An online shop is hit by a very large distributed denial of service attack from thousands of addresses. The company's internet link is completely full. What is the BEST action?
options: Add a rule on the company firewall for each attacking address
Activate the upstream scrubbing service named in the response plan
Add more memory and processors to the web servers
Restart the web servers and the firewall to clear all connections
examQuestions.explanation: When the link itself is full, traffic must be cleaned before it reaches the company, and following the agreed plan is the correct manager's response. Blocking addresses locally is tempting, but the flood has already filled the link by the time it reaches the firewall.

reviewSession.heading: How to approach this domain
reviewSession.body:
Let us go back over Domain 4 together, before the exam. This domain is about how information travels safely. Most questions come down to the same three steps. First, work out what is happening and where. Second, ask which layer the problem lives at. Third, choose the control that fixes the cause at that layer.

People often go wrong by picking the most impressive option. A strong control in the wrong place is still the wrong answer. Remember that you are an adviser and a manager. You follow policy, you think about business need and cost, you fix the cause and not the symptom, and you always put people's safety first. If an option involves ignoring a procedure or acting alone, then be suspicious of it. Keep these three steps in mind while we go through each area.

reviewSession.heading: The layers and encapsulation
reviewSession.body:
First, the layers, because they support everything else. From the top, the seven are Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link and Physical. The TCP IP model has four: Application, Transport, Internet and Network Access.

Going down the stack, the data unit names are data, segment, packet, frame and bits. Ports live at Layer 4. IP addresses and routers live at Layer 3. MAC addresses and switches live at Layer 2. Cables and hubs live at Layer 1.

People commonly mix up segment, packet and frame. Remember that the frame is the one with MAC addresses and an error-check trailer. TCP begins with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, and UDP has no handshake at all. When a question gives you a detail such as an address or a port, use that detail to name the layer before you read the options.

reviewSession.heading: IPsec and secure protocols
reviewSession.body:
Next, IPsec, which is very heavily tested. AH, the Authentication Header, proves origin and integrity, and it does not encrypt. ESP, the Encapsulating Security Payload, encrypts, and can also prove origin and integrity. Transport mode keeps the original IP header. Tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet in a new one.

So, if the question says that internal addresses must be hidden, you need ESP in tunnel mode. If it says that traffic passes through address translation, be careful with AH, because translation changes the header AH protects.

For other protocols, replace Telnet with SSH and retire SSL in favour of TLS 1.2 or 1.3. DNSSEC proves that answers are genuine but does not hide them. Know the common ports, especially 22, 23, 25, 53, 80, 389, 443, 636 and 3389.

reviewSession.heading: Wireless
reviewSession.body:
Now wireless. Remember the history in order. WEP is broken, WPA with TKIP was a stopgap, WPA2 uses AES with CCMP, and WPA3 Personal uses SAE, which resists offline guessing.

Personal means a shared password, and Enterprise means individual logins. So if a question is about accountability or removing one person's access, the answer is Enterprise with 802.1X.

The three 802.1X roles are often tested. The supplicant asks, the authenticator relays and enforces, and the authentication server decides. Do not think that the access point decides.

Hiding the network name and filtering MAC addresses are not real security. For Bluetooth, jacking is a nuisance, snarfing is theft and bugging is takeover. And for satellite and cellular links, remember that radio encryption stops at the provider, so protect sensitive data from end to end.

reviewSession.heading: Segmentation and modern design
reviewSession.body:
Next, how networks are divided. Segmentation limits how far an intruder can move. Physical segmentation uses separate equipment. In-band management shares the production network, out-of-band has a separate path, and an air gap has no connection at all.

Logical segmentation includes VLANs, VPNs, Virtual Routing and Forwarding, and virtual domains. A VLAN separates traffic, but it is not strong security on its own, and it needs a Layer 3 device to cross.

A pattern to watch for is an intruder who moves between servers while the perimeter firewall sees nothing. That is east-west traffic, and the answer is microsegmentation.

For software-defined networking, remember that it separates the control plane from the data plane, so the controller must be protected. For cloud, remember shared responsibility. Finally, bandwidth is capacity, throughput is real delivery, latency is delay and jitter is variation in delay.

reviewSession.heading: Firewalls and the devices on the path
reviewSession.body:
Now the devices. Learn the firewall types with their layers. A packet filter works at Layers 3 and 4, with no memory. A stateful firewall also works at Layers 3 and 4, and it remembers connections. A circuit-level gateway works at Layer 5. An application-level gateway works at Layer 7. A web application firewall works at Layer 7 and protects websites.

A common trap is SQL injection arriving on port 443. A port-based firewall will let it through, so you need a Layer 7 control, and the lasting fix is secure coding.

An IDS alerts and an IPS can block, because it is inline. A false negative is a missed attack, and it is usually the more dangerous error. Forward proxies serve clients, while reverse proxies serve servers. Firewall rules run from the top down, and the default is deny.

reviewSession.heading: Network access control and endpoints
reviewSession.body:
A short word on checking devices and protecting them. Network access control checks a device before it joins and continues checking while it is connected. A device that fails is sent to a quarantine network to be fixed, which lets the person keep working once it passes. If a question asks how to let approved people work while keeping unhealthy devices out, this is usually the answer.

Network access control comes as a physical or virtual solution, with or without an agent. Devices that cannot run an agent, such as cameras, belong in restricted zones.

Endpoint security means controls on the host itself. These include a host firewall, endpoint detection and response, disk encryption and patching. These matter because laptops leave the building, and perimeter controls cannot go with them. Remember too that a security device normally fails closed, unless a recorded risk decision says otherwise, particularly where safety is concerned.

reviewSession.heading: Media, power and availability
reviewSession.body:
Now the physical side. Copper Ethernet generally reaches 100 metres. Single-mode fiber goes long distances, and multimode stays closer. Fiber resists electrical interference, and it is harder to tap, but tapping is still possible. Plenum-rated cable is about keeping people safe from toxic smoke.

Learn the power words in pairs. Fault and blackout are loss of power. Sag and brownout are low voltage. Spike and surge are high voltage. In each pair, the first word is momentary and the second is prolonged.

The UPS must last longer than the generator takes to start. Availability equals mean time between failures, divided by the sum of mean time between failures and mean time to repair. A device that is past end of support is a risk to report to management early. A spare part does not fix missing security updates.

reviewSession.heading: Secure channels and third parties
reviewSession.body:
Next, how people and companies connect. For voice, SIP sets up the call and RTP carries the sound, so protect both, with SIP over TLS and SRTP. Remember that internet phones raise a safety question about emergency calls.

The key phrase for VPNs is that a tunnel is a road and not a lock. GRE has no encryption, L2TP needs IPsec and PPTP is obsolete. A full tunnel gives visibility, and a split tunnel saves bandwidth.

Administrator access needs multi-factor authentication, a hardened jump server, and logging. Do not expose the Remote Desktop Protocol to the internet.

For third parties, the answer is nearly always the same pattern. Access is approved, named, limited, time-bound, monitored and removed when the work ends. You can pass the work to someone else, but accountability stays with you. And a carrier's separation is not encryption.

reviewSession.heading: Attacks, from symptom to control
reviewSession.body:
Finally, attacks. The exam usually describes symptoms, so match the symptom to the name, and then to the control.

A full internet link means a volumetric attack, which must be cleaned upstream. Half-open connections with a link that is not full mean a SYN flood, and the answer is SYN cookies. A gateway address that maps to an ordinary computer means ARP poisoning, and the answer is Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping. A correct name that leads to a fake site suggests DNS poisoning, and the answer is DNSSEC. Sudden certificate warnings suggest an on-path attack.

Always check whether a tempting option actually addresses this attack. And during any incident, follow the plan, tell management and never attack back. Go through these once more, slowly, and trust what you have learned. You are ready to reason your way through these questions.
